name: Esther Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Esther. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name never goes with your answers. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hollis & Sons, a small insurer above the bank on the high street in our market town. There are fifteen of us, and we mostly insure farms: tractors, barns, cattle, crops against hail. I type up policies, send renewal letters, and take the first call when someone's barn roof comes off in a storm. I like that I know half the names on the files from church or school.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Learning the farm side. I grew up in town, so when a farmer rings about cover for his heifers or his grain dryer, I'm still writing it down to ask Mrs Pryce, our senior clerk, afterwards. I write my notes by hand and I don't use any of the AI programs; Mr Hollis doesn't push them either. I'm living at my parents' till the wedding next summer, so between that and what my fiancé Daniel and I put by, I've saved well over a year's costs. Daniel works at his family's bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I always thought it was mostly talk. People in the city get carried away. In a market town, folk want to speak to someone they know when their barn roof blows off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means life goes on as planned. Hollis & Sons has been there ninety years and doesn't change fast. If the big firms get a bit cheaper with their computers, we might lose a few customers, but farmers are loyal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and get better at the farm side, maybe go out with Mrs Pryce on a couple of farm visits so I actually know what a grain dryer looks like. Daniel and I would get married next summer as planned and put the deposit on a house. And I'd keep saving each month, same as my mother taught me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said farmers are loyal. Has anyone left for a big firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two families last year, for a cheaper price online. Mr Hollis took it personally. But one family came back to us after their claim took months with the online insurer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything worry you in this quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm's size, a bit. If Mr Hollis retires and his son doesn't want it, a big insurer might buy us. That worry was there before anyone said AI.

say: I'd say it was **mostly talk** from people in the city.
In a market town, folk want to speak to **someone they know**.
think: Life goes on **as planned**; the firm is ninety years old and slow to change.
Big firms may take **a few customers**, but farmers are loyal.
do: Join Mrs Pryce on **farm visits** to learn the equipment.
Marry Daniel next summer and put a **deposit on a house**.
Keep **saving each month** as her mother taught her.
S0.quote: In a market town, folk want to speak to someone they know when their barn roof blows off.
fieldNote: Esther's calm rests on a **small, old firm** and a loyal rural customer base.
She already carries a quiet worry about the owner **retiring and selling**.
Her values show early: **faith, family and thrift** frame every plan.

steps.text: Keep typing up farm policies at Hollis & Sons
Join Mrs Pryce on farm visits to learn the equipment
Put a deposit on a house with Daniel after the wedding
Keep saving part of each wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the big firms and the tech companies pushing this, not ordinary people asking for it. I'd say the answer is hard work and looking after your own, not waiting for the government. And I'd say a small firm that knows its customers is worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried for Hollis & Sons more than for me. If the big insurers can do quotes and claims in minutes with computers, farmers will drift to them on price, and a firm of fifteen can't afford to fall behind. And if Mr Hollis has to cut, the junior who won't touch the new programs goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work hard, and if Mr Hollis brought in a new system I'd learn it, though not happily. I'd hold off on the house for a year and put the deposit money aside instead. And I'd ask Daniel's father, quietly, whether the bakery could ever use another pair of hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. I pray about things like this, and it does help, but it's a weight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Hollis if he called you in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm loyal and I'll learn whatever he needs. I'd ask him for a few months to get used to it. He's a fair man; he gave me the job when I had no experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hard work, not government. If you lost the job, would you take government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not. If I lost my job, it'd be family first, then church, then the government if there's truly nothing else. My dad was out of work once for six months and we managed on family and the church food bank, and he never forgot who helped.

say: I'd say **big firms** and **tech companies** are pushing this, not ordinary people.
The answer is **hard work** and looking after your own.
think: I'm more worried for **Hollis & Sons** than for myself.
If cuts come, the junior who **won't touch new programs** goes first.
do: Learn any **new system** Mr Hollis brings in, reluctantly.
Delay the **house** by a year and keep the deposit aside.
Ask Daniel's father whether the **bakery** could use another pair of hands.
feel: **Anxious**, with prayer as a **comfort** that helps but doesn't lift the weight.
S1.quote: If I lost my job, it'd be family first, then church, then the government if there's truly nothing else.
fieldNote: Esther blames **big firms and tech**, and puts faith in hard work, not government.
She sees her **small employer** as the one at risk, with herself next in line.
Her order of help is clear: **family, church**, then government only as a last resort.

steps.text: Keep working hard and learn any system Mr Hollis brings in
Put the house purchase off by a year
Ask Daniel's father about work at the family bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast for decent people to keep up, and those who built it should be held to account. I'd say families and churches will have to carry each other. I wouldn't go on marches, but I'd say it plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is gone, I'm sure of it, and maybe the whole firm. If a computer can do any thinking work, a farmer can insure his tractor on his phone in a minute. What's left is the bakery, which is hands-on, so it has about three more years before robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go and work at Daniel's family bakery as soon as Hollis & Sons let me go, earlier if they offered. We'd bring the wedding forward to this spring, keep it small at the church hall, and put the rest of the money aside. I'd learn the bread side from Daniel's mother, early mornings and all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and a bit angry. I'm not built for this much change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring the wedding forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to be married and settled before everything goes upside down. A small wedding at the church hall is still a wedding. My mother would cry about the guest list, but she'd understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the robots for bakeries around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. People here buy their bread from the Brennans because they know the family, not because it's cheapest, and maybe that lasts. If it doesn't, I'll trust God and my family, because I don't have a better plan.

say: I'd say it's going **too fast** for decent people, and its makers must answer for it.
**Families and churches** will have to carry each other.
think: My job is **gone**, and maybe the **whole firm**.
The **bakery** is hands-on, so it has about three more years before robots.
do: Join Daniel's **family bakery** once Hollis & Sons lets her go.
Bring the **wedding forward** to spring, small, at the church hall.
Learn the **bread side** from Daniel's mother.
feel: Feels she is **not built** for this much change.
S2.quote: A small wedding at the church hall is still a wedding.
fieldNote: Fast AGI pushes Esther straight to her **fiancé's family business**.
Bringing the **wedding forward** is her way of anchoring her life before the upheaval.
She has **no plan after 2031** and openly leans on faith and family.

steps.text: Start work at Daniel's family bakery once laid off
Bring the wedding forward to spring at the church hall
Learn bread-making from Daniel's mother on early shifts
Put the leftover wedding money aside

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people to prepare, if they're sensible and don't wait for someone else to fix it. Firms should be honest with their staff about dates. I'd say look after your family and learn something useful with your hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job goes around 2030, and Hollis & Sons may sell up before that. Five years gives me time to get married properly and learn a trade at the bakery while I still have a wage. The bakery buys a few more years, until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Hollis & Sons and help at the bakery on Saturdays from next year, learning the ovens and the early shifts. We'd marry next summer as planned and maybe buy a smaller house so we don't over-stretch. I'd keep a full year's costs in the bank no matter what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. Knowing it's coming gives me time to pray on it and plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Saturdays at the bakery. What's that like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four in the morning, flour everywhere, Daniel singing badly. I've done it a few times at Christmas. I'm slow, but his mother says I've got patient hands for pastry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use the AI programs, with five years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, to be honest. I'd rather spend the next five years learning bread at a bakery than learning computer programs that will replace me anyway. That might be stubborn, and my sister tells me it is.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough if people don't wait for someone else.
Firms should be honest about dates, and families should learn **hands-on skills**.
think: My job goes around **2030**, and the firm may **sell up** sooner.
The bakery buys time until about **2034**.
do: Help at the **bakery on Saturdays** from next year.
Marry next summer and buy a **smaller house**.
Keep a **full year's costs** in the bank no matter what.
feel: **Anxious but steadier**, with time to pray on it and plan.
S3.quote: I'd rather spend the next five years learning bread at a bakery than learning computer programs that will replace me anyway.
fieldNote: Five years lets Esther **keep her wedding plans** and build a bakery skill slowly.
She **refuses AI tools** even with warning, preferring skills that last past 2031.
A **year of costs** in the bank is her fixed rule.

steps.text: Keep working at Hollis & Sons while the wage lasts
Learn the ovens at the bakery every Saturday from next year
Buy a smaller house after the wedding next summer
Keep a full year of costs in the bank

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so nobody should be wringing their hands. Work hard, learn a trade, look after your family. That's what I'd say at church and at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd be 37 and probably have children by then. I'd want to be settled in work that robots don't take until about 2039. The insurance job probably goes, but not before I've had a good run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hollis & Sons for a few more years and learn the farm side properly. We'd marry and start a family on our own timetable. Later on, I'd move into the bakery with Daniel, maybe around 2032, so the business has two of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly at peace. The Lord's given us time in that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about having children in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether they'd have work at all. I'd want my children to learn something with their hands, the way my fiancé Daniel did. But I can't plan their whole lives; I'll just raise them right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Hollis about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to sell while the firm's still worth something, if his son doesn't want it. He'd hate hearing that from a junior. But someone should say it.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty, so no hand-wringing.
Work hard, learn a **trade** and look after your **family**.
think: I'd be **37**, probably with **children**, when thinking AI arrives.
The insurance job goes, but not before a **good run**.
do: Learn the **farm side** properly at Hollis & Sons for a few years.
Marry and start a **family** on their own timetable.
Move into the **bakery** with Daniel around 2032.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly **at peace**, grateful for the time.
S4.quote: I'd want my children to learn something with their hands, the way my fiancé Daniel did.
fieldNote: A decade lets Esther keep **family first**: marriage and children on her own timetable.
She'd tell her boss to **sell the firm** while it's still worth something.
Her future children's work is the **new worry** this picture brings.

steps.text: Stay at Hollis & Sons and learn farm cover properly
Marry Daniel and start a family on their own timetable
Move into Daniel's family bakery around 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It would take my job and our town's insurer before I'd even be married, and I'm not someone who changes quickly. What would help is family and church pulling together, and if the government does anything, I'd want it to pay for apprenticeships, not just hand out money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the farmers. When a barn burns down, the family wants somebody who'll drive out and stand in the yard with them. A computer can't do that, at least not yet.

headlineQuote: When a barn burns down, the family wants somebody who'll drive out and stand in the yard with them.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old clerk** at a small family-owned farm insurer in a market town.
She avoids AI, writes notes **by hand**, and is still learning farm terms.
Engaged to Daniel, a baker, she has **over a year saved** while living with her parents.
She trusts **family and church** before government and favours apprenticeships over handouts.
Her mood runs from **calm** to **alarmed**, and her fallback is always the **family bakery**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would take her job and the town's insurer before her wedding.
